definition: Repulse means to drive back an attack or advance, forcing it to retreat.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word repulse. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know repulse should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Guard bees massed at the hive entrance and repulsed the hornet three times before it finally gave up.
Resist is milder than repulse — the line strains and holds its ground, the outcome undecided — while repulse sends the attack back the way it came.
Crush goes further than repulse — a repulsed force retreats in order and may try again, while a crushed one is finished as a force at all.

To repel is the near-twin with a wider day job — a magnet repels its match, spray repels insects, and no battle is required anywhere. Repulse is the sharper military word: it wants an actual attack or advance in the sentence, coming on and being driven back.

Beat back is the plain, everyday phrase for turning back an advancing force in a real struggle — firefighters beat back flames, defenders beat back a charge. Repulse says the same thing in formal military register: the historian's word for an assault driven off.

Repulse means to drive back an attack or advance, forcing it to retreat.
For eighty years the mountain's north ridge repulsed everyone who tried it.
Storms turned parties around at the shoulder; ice sheeted the one workable chimney; a rope team in 1963 got within four hundred feet and was driven down by wind that peeled a tent from its anchors.
The ridge did not care how good anyone was.
It sent them all back down.
Repulse is the exact word for what the ridge did, because it means to drive back, to repel an attack or advance — the push comes on, and force sends it back the way it came.
Resist would only say the mountain held; repulse says the climbers ended up back where they started.
Repulse is the battlefield verb: an advance comes on and is driven back — armies, raids, surges, takeover bids.
Repel is its near-twin with a wider day job (fabrics repel water; spray repels insects); when the sentence contains an attack, repulse hits harder.
It also has a second life — 'his table manners repulsed her' — but this unit's sense is the military one.
Among the unit's disapproval words, repudiate rejects claims and reprove corrects people; repulse alone stops a charge.

The museum's new exhibit centers on a single night in 1746, when the garrison of Fort Belmont -- ninety men, half of them sick -- faced a force six times their size.
The attackers came up the ravine twice before midnight.

Twice the defenders repulsed them, and the fort's log records the second retreat in one dry line: 'the enemy fell back to the tree line and did not re-form.' Visitors sometimes misread the famous line, assuming the defenders felt disgust at their enemy.
The curator's placard corrects them: the word here is military, not emotional -- it means the assault was met, turned, and driven back down the slope.
A third attack never came, and by spring the ravine road was a cattle path again.
